candidates.quote: Blessed be God, at the end of the last year I was in very good health, without any sense of my old pain, but upon taking of cold.
candidates.author: Samuel Pepys
candidates.locator: the opening entry, January 1659/60, ed. Henry B. Wheatley, vol. I (George Bell, 1893)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous diary in English opens by taking stock at the turn of the year, glad of good health and ready to begin, which is the December reckoning in a single breath.

candidates.quote: After the wet dark days, the country seems more populous. It peoples itself in the sunbeams. The garden, mimic of spring, is gay with flowers.
candidates.author: Dorothy Wordsworth
candidates.locator: the opening entry, 20 January 1798, Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth, ed. William Knight, vol. I (Macmillan, 1897)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written in the dead of winter, it catches the garden already rehearsing spring, which is renewal noticed before it has fully arrived.

candidates.quote: Since it has pleased Providence to place me in this station, I shall do my utmost to fulfil my duty towards my country; I am very young and perhaps in many, though not in all things, inexperienced, but I am sure that very few have more real goodwill and more real desire to do what is fit and right than I have.
candidates.author: Queen Victoria
candidates.locator: 20 June 1837, the day of her accession, extract printed in The Letters of Queen Victoria, vol. I, ch. VI, 1837 (ed. A. C. Benson and Viscount Esher, John Murray, 1907)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Woken at six to be told she was queen, a girl of eighteen writes down her resolve before breakfast: a beginning met with good will rather than fear.

candidates.quote: We should be willing to act as a balm for all wounds.
candidates.author: Etty Hillesum
candidates.work: An Interrupted Life: The Diaries of Etty Hillesum 1941 to 1943
candidates.locator: the closing sentence of the diaries, October 1942
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last sentence of her diaries asks nothing for herself and offers healing to everyone, which is hope turned outward at the darkest hour.

candidates.quote: You can not now realize that you will ever feel better. Is not this so? And yet it is a mistake. You are sure to be happy again.
candidates.author: Abraham Lincoln
candidates.locator: 23 December 1862, Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Roy P. Basler, vol. 6 (Rutgers University Press, 1953)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two days before Christmas a president writes to a grieving girl that she will be happy again, and says he knows it from experience: hope promised by someone who has earned the right.

candidates.quote: My heart is singing for joy this morning. A miracle has happened! The light of understanding has shone upon my little pupil’s mind, and behold, all things are changed!
candidates.author: Anne Sullivan
candidates.locator: 20 March 1887, printed in Helen Keller, The Story of My Life, Part III, ch. III, Education (Doubleday, Page, 1903)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A teacher writes on the morning everything changed for her pupil, a reminder that renewal arrives on an ordinary morning after long patient work.

candidates.quote: I will seize Fate by the throat; it shall certainly not bend and crush me completely—Oh, it would be so lovely to live a thousand lives.
candidates.author: Ludwig van Beethoven
candidates.locator: 16 November 1801, The Letters of Beethoven, vol. I (Macmillan, 1961)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Writing to an old friend as his hearing failed, the composer answers with an appetite for life rather than surrender, which is hope as a decision taken in the morning.

candidates.quote: Hang on to your hat. Hang on to your hope. And wind the clock, for tomorrow is another day.
candidates.author: E. B. White
candidates.locator: 30 March 1973, the closing sentences, Letters of E. B. White, ed. Dorothy Lobrano Guth (Harper and Row, 1976)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The close of a letter to a stranger who had lost heart gives three plain instructions for keeping hope, and the last of them is a morning chore.

candidates.quote: Live, then, and be happy, beloved children of my heart, and never forget that until the day when God shall deign to reveal the future to man, all human wisdom is summed up in these two words,—‘Wait and hope.’
candidates.author: Alexandre Dumas
candidates.locator: chapter 117, The Fifth of October, the Count’s farewell letter to Maximilian Morrel and Valentine
candidates.whyThisMonth: A thousand pages of revenge close on two gentle words, and they are the ones worth carrying out of the door into a new day.
candidates.speaker: Edmond Dantès, Count of Monte Cristo, in his letter

candidates.quote: He rustled his feathers and held his slender neck high, as he cried out with full heart: ‘I never dreamed there could be so much happiness, when I was the ugly duckling.’
candidates.author: Hans Christian Andersen
candidates.whyThisMonth: The tale ends with the lilacs out and a creature who at last knows what it is, which is renewal told so simply a child can hold it.
candidates.speaker: the ugly duckling, now a swan

candidates.quote: Here was peace. She pulled in her horizon like a great fish-net. Pulled it from around the waist of the world and draped it over her shoulder. So much of life in its meshes! She called in her soul to come and see.
candidates.author: Zora Neale Hurston
candidates.locator: chapter 20, the closing sentences (J. B. Lippincott, 1937)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The novel’s last lines gather a whole life in like a net and find it full, an ending that feels like room to begin again.

candidates.quote: At first people refuse to believe that a strange new thing can be done, then they begin to hope it can be done, then they see it can be done—then it is done and all the world wonders why it was not done centuries ago.
candidates.author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
candidates.locator: chapter XXVII, In the Garden, the opening paragraph of the last chapter (Frederick A. Stokes, 1911)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last chapter of a book about a garden coming back to life opens by tracing how every new thing passes from impossible to hoped for to obvious.

candidates.quote: ‘Now I’ve got everything,’ Moomintroll said to himself. ‘I’ve got the whole year. Winter too. I’m the first Moomin to have lived through an entire year.’
candidates.author: Tove Jansson
candidates.locator: chapter 6, The First of Spring, the line at which the narrator says the tale ought to stop, before a short coda
candidates.whyThisMonth: Having stayed awake through the whole long winter, Moomintroll finds that he owns the year, spring included, which is December’s promise in a book for children.
candidates.speaker: Moomintroll

candidates.quote: Hope is definitely not the same thing as optimism. It is not the conviction that something will turn out well, but the certainty that something makes sense, regardless of how it turns out.
candidates.author: Václav Havel
candidates.work: Disturbing the Peace: A Conversation with Karel Hvížďala
candidates.locator: p. 181 (Alfred A. Knopf, 1990); Havel wrote his answers in 1985 and the book appeared in Czech in 1986
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written by a dissident who could not know how things would turn out, it separates hope from forecasting, which is the only kind of hope a dark month can keep.

candidates.quote: In the middle of winter I at last discovered that there was in me an invincible summer.
candidates.author: Albert Camus
candidates.locator: near the close of the essay, in Summer (1954); The Myth of Sisyphus and Other Essays (Alfred A. Knopf, 1955)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The darkest season is where he found the summer he carried inside him, the plainest December line there is.

candidates.quote: Patience, patience, patience, is what the sea teaches. Patience and faith. One should lie empty, open, choiceless as a beach—waiting for a gift from the sea.
candidates.author: Anne Morrow Lindbergh
candidates.whyThisMonth: Her small book about a woman renewing herself begins by counselling patience, the kind that waits with open hands for whatever the tide brings.
